# The AWS map: global infrastructure, shared responsibility, Well-Architected: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=aws-map-q008 -->
### Question 1

A company is expanding into a new country where an AWS Region exists. A new law requires that the personal data of customers in that country must remain in the country. The company will store the data in Amazon S3 and process it on Amazon EC2 instances. Other AWS Regions nearby offer lower prices. Which solution will ensure data residency with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create the S3 bucket and the EC2 instances in the Region in that country, and do not turn on any cross-Region replication or copy feature.
- Create the resources in the Region in that country, and turn off the account setting that lets AWS copy data to other Regions.
- Create the resources in a lower-priced Region in a neighboring country, because that Region is the nearest one with lower prices.
- Create the resources in the Region in that country, and run a scheduled job that deletes any copies of the data in other Regions.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create the S3 bucket and the EC2 instances in the Region in that country, and do not turn on any cross-Region replication or copy feature.

**Deciding phrases.** "must remain in the country", "ensure data residency", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that will ensure data residency with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: the personal data must remain in one country, that country has an AWS Region, and the data lives in Amazon S3 and on EC2 instances. The lower prices nearby are bait.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict: create everything in the Region in that country and add no replication, because AWS stores customer content in the Region where I use the service.
4. I remove the neighboring Region, because the data would sit in another country. I remove the account setting, because there is no such setting: AWS does not copy my data to another Region unless I use a replication or copy feature.
5. Between the plain deployment and the deployment with a cleanup job, the difference is extra work; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, and the job deletes copies that do not exist, so I choose the plain deployment.
6. Check: the Region in that country with no replication meets the law, needs no job, and needs no setting. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** AWS services [process and store customer content in the AWS region(s) where the services are used by the customer](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-customer-content-stays-in-chosen-region). So the data stays in the Region in that country as long as the company adds no replication or copy feature. No extra setting or job is needed.

**Why not.**

- "Create the resources in the Region in that ...": There is nothing to turn off: AWS keeps resources out of other Regions [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).
- "Create the resources in a lower-priced Region in ...": The services [process and store customer content in the AWS region(s) where the services are used by the customer](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-customer-content-stays-in-chosen-region), so the data would sit in the other country.
- "Create the resources in the Region in that ...": The job adds work with no effect, because no copy exists in another Region [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).

**Twin.** If the stem said "any European Union Region meets the law" and "MOST cost-effective" instead: the lowest-priced of those Regions, because prices are [different in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-pricing-differs-local-market).

**Takeaway.** Data stays in the Region you choose unless you configure replication or copying yourself.

**Review.** [Each request goes to one Region and your resources stay there](2-deep.md#each-request-goes-to-one-region-and-your-resources-stay-there-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an order-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances. The company chose the Linux operating system of the instances when it launched them. A new security engineer reviews the AWS shared responsibility model to plan the work of the security team. A vendor publishes a security patch for a vulnerability in that Linux operating system. Which task is the responsibility of the company?

- Apply security patches to the virtualization layer of the physical hosts that run the EC2 instances.
- Control physical access to the data center facilities that hold the hosts that run the EC2 instances.
- Apply the security patch to the guest operating system that runs on each of the EC2 instances.
- Ask AWS to apply the security patch to the guest operating system in the next maintenance window.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Apply the security patch to the guest operating system that runs on each of the EC2 instances.

**Deciding phrases.** "Amazon EC2 instances", "a security patch for a vulnerability in that Linux operating system"

**Why.** Patch management is a shared control. [AWS is responsible for patching and fixing flaws within the infrastructure](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control), and [customers are responsible for patching their guest OS and applications](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-patch-management-is-a-shared-control). The company chose the operating system on its instances, so the company applies the patch.

**Why not.**

- "Apply security patches to the virtualization layer of ...": AWS controls the components [from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-aws-controls-host-os-virtualization-and-facilities).
- "Control physical access to the data center facilities ...": Facilities are part of the infrastructure, and AWS protects [the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS Cloud services](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-aws-responsible-for-infrastructure-security-of-the-cloud).
- "Ask AWS to apply the security patch to ...": EC2 is [categorized as Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-ec2-is-iaas-customer-does-all-security-configuration), so AWS does not patch the guest operating system for the company.

**Twin.** If the stem said "tables in Amazon DynamoDB" instead: AWS will [apply patches without requiring customer action](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-multi-tenant-managed-services-aws-patches-without-customer-action), and the company's task becomes [using IAM tools to apply the appropriate permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-shared-responsibility-customer-applies-permissions-with-iam).

**Takeaway.** On EC2, AWS patches the infrastructure and the customer patches the guest operating system.

**Review.** [AWS secures the cloud and you secure what you put in it](2-deep.md#aws-secures-the-cloud-and-you-secure-what-you-put-in-it-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company stores product images in one Amazon S3 bucket in a single AWS Region. A web application in the same Region shows the images to users around the world. Users far from the Region report that pages load slowly because the images take a long time to download. The images change once a week, and the application itself responds fast. Which solution will improve the download times for these users with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Copy the S3 bucket and the web application to several AWS Regions, and route each user to the nearest Region with Amazon Route 53 latency routing.
- Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and serve the images to the users through the distribution.
- Enable a Local Zone in each city where users report slow pages, and run copies of the application and the image storage there.
- Move the images to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access storage class, and turn on S3 Versioning to keep each weekly change.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and serve the images to the users through the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "users around the world", "the images take a long time to download", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, AWS Firewall Manager, AWS Shield, and AWS WAF services are provided through AWS Edge Locations](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-edge-location-services). A CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket serves the images from edge locations near the users. The bucket, the Region and the application do not change.

**Why not.**

- "Copy the S3 bucket and the web application ...": It works, but in a multi-Region design [you must duplicate your workload's components in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-duplicate-everything-no-cross-region-dependency), which adds far more operational work.
- "Enable a Local Zone in each city where ...": Local Zones bring [the core services needed for the latency-sensitive portions of your workload](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-vs-availability-zones-core-vs-full-services) close to users, but a copy in every city adds much more work.
- "Move the images to the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access ...": The images still download from the one Region, so the distance to the users and the slow pages stay the same.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users in one city run an interactive application on EC2" instead: a Local Zone, because it suits workloads that need [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-single-digit-millisecond-latency-workloads).

**Takeaway.** Static content for users around the world: put CloudFront in front of the bucket.

**Review.** [Edge locations serve users nearby and Local Zones run compute near them](2-deep.md#edge-locations-serve-users-nearby-and-local-zones-run-compute-near-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The application keeps no state on the instances, and users reach it through one DNS name. After several short outages, the company wants a more reliable design. The application must remain available if an Availability Zone fails. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Run the instances in two Availability Zones of the current Region behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones.
- Run a second copy of the application in another AWS Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing with health checks to send users to the healthy copy.
- Run active copies of the application in three AWS Regions at the same time, and use Amazon Route 53 latency routing with health checks to send each user to a copy.
- Add more instances in the current Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that replaces any unhealthy instance.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the instances in two Availability Zones of the current Region behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones.

**Deciding phrases.** "in one Availability Zone", "if an Availability Zone fails", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** An EC2 instance is a zonal resource, [specific to the Availability Zone in which you create it](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-zonal-resource-deploy-in-multiple-azs). AWS says to [deploy your application in multiple Availability Zones, so that your application remains available even if one Availability Zone fails](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-zonal-resource-deploy-in-multiple-azs). A second zone in the same Region adds a few instances and a load balancer, which costs less than a copy in another Region.

**Why not.**

- "Run a second copy of the application in ...": It also survives a zone failure, but it pays for a full copy in a second Region, and [most customers can achieve their resilience goals in a single Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-most-customers-single-region-suffices).
- "Run active copies of the application in three ...": Three active Regions survive a zone failure, but AWS names this anti-pattern: [you implement a multi-Region architecture when a multi-AZ architecture would satisfy business requirements](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-when-multi-az-suffices-is-anti-pattern).
- "Add more instances in the current Availability Zone ...": If all instances are in one zone and that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), however many instances run there.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must remain available if the AWS Region fails" instead: the second copy in another Region, because the separation between Regions [avoids correlated failures between them](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-avoids-correlated-failures).

**Takeaway.** A zone failure calls for two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, not a second Region.

**Review.** [Availability Zones fail separately so production uses at least two](2-deep.md#availability-zones-fail-separately-so-production-uses-at-least-two-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=aws-map-q007 -->
### Question 5

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The application keeps no state on the instances, and users reach it through one DNS name. After several short outages, the company wants a more reliable design. The application must remain available if the AWS Region fails. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Run the instances in two Availability Zones of the current Region behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones.
- Run a second copy of the application in another AWS Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing with health checks to send users to the healthy copy.
- Run active copies of the application in three AWS Regions at the same time, and use Amazon Route 53 latency routing with health checks to send each user to a copy.
- Add more instances in the current Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Auto Scaling group that replaces any unhealthy instance.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run a second copy of the application in another AWS Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing with health checks to send users to the healthy copy.

**Deciding phrases.** "in one Availability Zone", "if the AWS Region fails", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Each Region is [designed to be isolated from the other Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance), and that separation [avoids correlated failures between them](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-avoids-correlated-failures). A copy in a second Region keeps serving when the first Region fails, and Route 53 health checks send users to it. One standby copy costs less than active copies in three Regions.

**Why not.**

- "Run the instances in two Availability Zones of ...": Two zones survive a zone failure, but both zones sit inside the failed Region, so the application stops with that Region.
- "Run active copies of the application in three ...": Three active Regions also survive the failure, but they run three full copies where one copy in a second Region meets the requirement.
- "Add more instances in the current Availability Zone ...": If that one zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), and a Region failure takes that zone too.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must remain available if an Availability Zone fails" instead: two Availability Zones behind a load balancer, because [most customers can achieve their resilience goals in a single Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-most-customers-single-region-suffices).

**Takeaway.** A Region failure needs a copy in a second Region; the zones of the failed Region fail with it.

**Review.** [A second Region protects against Region failure but replicates asynchronously](2-deep.md#a-second-region-protects-against-region-failure-but-replicates-asynchronously-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs an interactive design application on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. Most users work in one large city that is far from every AWS Region. The application processes each user action in real time, and the users report slow responses. The company wants to run the EC2 instances closer to users and needs single-digit millisecond latency for them. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for these users?

- Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the Regional EC2 instances as the origin, so that users connect to an edge location.
- Move the EC2 instances to the AWS Region that is nearest to the city, and keep the current Region as a warm standby.
- Move the application to larger EC2 instance types with more vCPUs in the current Region to process each action faster.
- Enable a Local Zone near the city, create a subnet in that Local Zone, and run the EC2 instances in that subnet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable a Local Zone near the city, create a subnet in that Local Zone, and run the EC2 instances in that subnet.

**Deciding phrases.** "one large city that is far from every AWS Region", "single-digit millisecond latency", "LOWEST latency"

**Why.** Local Zones are designed for workloads that need [single-digit millisecond latency](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-local-zones-single-digit-millisecond-latency-workloads). A Local Zone is [an extension of an AWS Region in geographic proximity to your users](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zone-extension-of-region-own-internet), so the EC2 instances run near the city instead of in a distant Region.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the Regional ...": Edge locations host [Amazon CloudFront](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-pop-hosts-cloudfront-route53-global-accelerator), but each user action is still processed on the instances in the distant Region.
- "Move the EC2 instances to the AWS Region ...": It lowers latency, but the nearest Region is still far from the city, while Local Zones sit [close to large population and industry centers](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zones-definition-close-to-population-centers).
- "Move the application to larger EC2 instance types ...": Larger instances shorten the processing time, but the network distance between the city and the Region stays the same.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users connect from 5G mobile devices on one carrier network" instead: AWS Wavelength, because it is designed for [ultralow-latency applications to 5G devices](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-wavelength-ultralow-latency-for-5g-devices).

**Takeaway.** Compute near the users of one city runs in a Local Zone; CloudFront at the edge does not move the compute.

**Review.** [Edge locations serve users nearby and Local Zones run compute near them](2-deep.md#edge-locations-serve-users-nearby-and-local-zones-run-compute-near-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs a managed relational database for an order system in one AWS Region. The database must lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails. If the whole Region fails, the company must be able to recover the database in a second Region, and a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with synchronous replication from the primary database.
- Take a snapshot of the database every few minutes, and keep all of the snapshots in the same AWS Region as the database.
- Keep a replica of the database in a second AWS Region, with asynchronous replication from the primary database in the first Region.
- Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with asynchronous replication every few minutes.
- Run a self-managed database on EC2 instances in a second AWS Region, and write a custom process that ships the changes every minute.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Keep a standby copy of the database in a second Availability Zone of the Region, with synchronous replication from the primary database.
- Keep a replica of the database in a second AWS Region, with asynchronous replication from the primary database in the first Region.

**Deciding phrases.** "lose no committed write if an Availability Zone fails", "a loss of a few minutes of writes is acceptable", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two failures need two copies. The zones are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms), so the standby keeps every committed write. The replica in a second Region is asynchronous, which the stem accepts.

- The zones of a Region are close enough to [replicate data synchronously between Availability Zones](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-latency-single-digit-ms), so the standby holds every committed write.
- The Region copy is asynchronous, and the stem accepts [the possibility of data loss or inconsistency when you fail over](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-async-cross-region-replication-may-lose-data) of a few minutes.

**Why not.**

- "Take a snapshot of the database every few ...": The snapshots stay in the failed Region, because no copy exists in another Region [unless you explicitly use a replication or copy feature offered by an AWS service or replicate the resource yourself](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-no-automatic-cross-region-replication).
- "Keep a standby copy of the database in ...": Asynchronous replication can leave the newest writes behind, so a zone failure can lose committed writes that the stem does not allow.
- "Run a self-managed database on EC2 instances in ...": It can meet the few minutes of loss, but a self-managed database and a custom process add far more operational work than a managed replica.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a Region failure must lose no committed write" instead: the asynchronous replica no longer meets it, because it brings [the possibility of data loss or inconsistency when you fail over](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-async-cross-region-replication-may-lose-data).

**Takeaway.** Synchronous standby in a second zone for zero loss; asynchronous replica in a second Region for a short loss.

**Review.** [A second Region protects against Region failure but replicates asynchronously](2-deep.md#a-second-region-protects-against-region-failure-but-replicates-asynchronously-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs a latency-sensitive application in AWS account A and its database in AWS account B, in the us-east-1 Region. Both accounts were created in 2021. The VPCs of the two accounts are connected, and each account creates subnets in its own VPC. The company wants the application instances and the database in the same physical Availability Zone. The engineers in each account choose zones by the names that their own console shows, such as us-east-1a. The company must ensure that both workloads use the same physical zone. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create the application subnet in the zone that has the same Availability Zone name, such as us-east-1a, as the database subnet in the other account.
- Move the application and the database into one AWS account, so that both workloads see the same zone names for the same physical zones.
- Open an AWS Support case to ask AWS to map the Availability Zone names of both accounts to the same physical zones.
- Look up the AZ ID of the database subnet, such as use1-az2, and create the application subnet in the zone with the same AZ ID.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Look up the AZ ID of the database subnet, such as use1-az2, and create the application subnet in the zone with the same AZ ID.

**Deciding phrases.** "choose zones by the names that their own console shows", "ensure that both workloads use the same physical zone", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** An Availability Zone ID (AZ ID) names [the same physical location in every AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-id-same-physical-location-every-account). Each team looks up the AZ ID of the database zone and creates its subnet in the zone with the matching AZ ID. This needs no move between accounts and no support case.

**Why not.**

- "Create the application subnet in the zone that ...": For accounts created before November 2025, a zone name [might not be the same physical location as it is in another account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-name-mapping-independent-per-account), so matching names does not ensure one physical zone.
- "Move the application and the database into one ...": It can work, but moving a workload between accounts is far more work than reading one zone attribute in each account.
- "Open an AWS Support case to ask AWS ...": No support case is needed, because an AZ ID already names [the same physical location in every AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-id-same-physical-location-every-account).

**Twin.** If the stem said "both workloads run in one AWS account" instead: the zone name is enough, because AWS maps names per account: [we independently map Availability Zones to codes for each AWS account](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-az-name-mapping-independent-per-account).

**Takeaway.** Across accounts, match Availability Zones by AZ ID, not by zone name.

**Review.** [Availability Zones fail separately so production uses at least two](2-deep.md#availability-zones-fail-separately-so-production-uses-at-least-two-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a mission-critical web tier on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The Region has three Availability Zones. Load tests show that the tier needs six instances to serve peak traffic. The tier must keep full peak capacity during the failure of one Availability Zone. Which design will meet these requirements and be the MOST resilient?

- Run nine instances, three in each Availability Zone, so that the two remaining zones still hold six running instances after one zone fails.
- Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, and let the Auto Scaling group launch replacement instances in the other zones after a zone failure.
- Run six instances in the Availability Zone with the most free capacity, and let the Auto Scaling group replace any unhealthy instance in that zone.
- Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, and keep a copy of the tier with no running instances in a second AWS Region.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run nine instances, three in each Availability Zone, so that the two remaining zones still hold six running instances after one zone fails.

**Deciding phrases.** "needs six instances to serve peak traffic", "keep full peak capacity during the failure of one Availability Zone", "MOST resilient"

**Why.** A statically stable design can [continue to operate as normal without the need to make changes during the failure or unavailability of dependencies](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-static-stability-definition). The AWS example deploys [three instances in each Availability Zone, for a total of nine](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-static-stability-example-three-per-az-fifty-percent), so a zone failure leaves the full capacity running.

**Why not.**

- "Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, ...": Replacements come late, because [launching new EC2 instances takes time](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-auto-scaling-relies-on-ec2-control-plane) and [deploying new instances through auto scaling relies on the EC2 control plane](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-auto-scaling-relies-on-ec2-control-plane).
- "Run six instances in the Availability Zone with ...": If that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances), so the tier loses all of its capacity.
- "Run six instances, two in each Availability Zone, ...": A standby Region answers a Region failure; during a zone failure, the tier runs on four instances until new instances launch.

**Twin.** If the stem said "can run at reduced capacity for an hour after a zone failure" instead: six instances across three zones with Auto Scaling, because the tier can wait while replacements launch.

**Takeaway.** To keep full capacity through a zone failure (fault tolerance), pre-provision the spare capacity in the other zones.

**Review.** [Availability Zones fail separately so production uses at least two](2-deep.md#availability-zones-fail-separately-so-production-uses-at-least-two-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company runs its production workload on Amazon EC2 instances in the Asia Pacific (Sydney) Region to serve users in Australia. The engineers also work in Sydney. The company needs a new development and test environment that holds only synthetic test data. The company has no data privacy, security, or business requirements about where the environment runs, and extra latency for the engineers is not a concern. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Run the development and test EC2 instances in the Asia Pacific (Sydney) Region, next to the production workload of the company.
- Run the development and test EC2 instances in a Local Zone near the office of the engineers to give them lower latency.
- Run the development and test EC2 instances in a Region with lower prices than Sydney, such as US East (N. Virginia).
- Run the development and test EC2 instances on AWS Outposts in the office of the company, so that the test data stays on premises.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the development and test EC2 instances in a Region with lower prices than Sydney, such as US East (N. Virginia).

**Deciding phrases.** "no data privacy, security, or business requirements", "is not a concern", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** AWS says to [use Regions that provide lower prices for AWS services to deploy your workloads if you have no obligations in data privacy, security and business requirements](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-cheaper-region-for-non-critical-when-no-restrictions). The stem removes each of those obligations and says latency is not a concern, so price decides the Region.

**Why not.**

- "Run the development and test EC2 instances in ...": It works, but resource prices are [different in each Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-pricing-differs-local-market), and nothing in the stem requires Sydney.
- "Run the development and test EC2 instances in ...": The stem says latency is not a concern. A Local Zone is [an extension of an AWS Region in geographic proximity to your users](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-local-zone-extension-of-region-own-internet), so it buys latency, not a lower price.
- "Run the development and test EC2 instances on ...": Outposts is for [workloads that need to remain on premises due to latency requirements](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-faq-outposts-for-workloads-that-must-stay-on-premises), and this test environment has no such requirement.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the test data includes customer records that must stay in Australia" instead: the Sydney Region, because AWS says to [only deploy in Regions with higher costs to meet latency, data residency and data sovereignty requirements](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-region-pricing-differs-choose-by-cost).

**Takeaway.** With no residency, security, or latency need, choose the lower-priced Region for development and test.

**Review.** [The best Region is near your users and meets your data rules](2-deep.md#the-best-region-is-near-your-users-and-meets-your-data-rules-4-min)

</details>
